questions.text: In immediate addressing mode, the operand is

options.text: in a register named by the instruction
at the memory address named by the instruction
at the address held in a register

questions.solution: The value is part of the instruction word, so no further access is needed once the instruction is fetched. That makes it the fastest mode and also the least flexible, since the value is fixed at assembly time.

questions.text: Which addressing mode is most suitable for stepping through the successive elements of an array?
questions.solution: Indexed addressing adds an index register to a base address, so advancing through the array is a matter of incrementing the index while the instruction stays the same.

questions.text: The instruction MOV R1, (R2) copies into R1 the contents of the memory location whose address is in R2. Which addressing mode does the source operand use?
questions.solution: The register holds an address rather than the value, so it is register indirect. This is how pointers are implemented at the machine level.

questions.text: In memory-indirect addressing, how many memory accesses are needed to obtain the operand, not counting the instruction fetch?
questions.solution: The first access reads the pointer from the address in the instruction; the second reads the operand from the address just obtained. Register indirect needs only one, because the pointer is already in a register.

questions.text: An instruction is 24 bits long and contains three operand fields, each identifying one of 32 registers. How many bits are left for the opcode?
questions.solution: 32 registers need 5 bits each, so the three fields take 15 bits, leaving 24 - 15 = 9 bits for the opcode.

questions.text: In a machine using zero-address instructions, where do the operands come from?

options.text: General purpose registers named by the instruction

questions.solution: A zero-address instruction names no operand because both are implicit: they are popped from the stack and the result is pushed back. Expressions are written in postfix form for such machines.

questions.text: A one-address instruction implicitly uses which register for the second operand and the result?
questions.solution: One-address machines name a single memory operand and take the other from the accumulator, leaving the result there too.

questions.text: Which phase begins every instruction cycle?
questions.solution: The instruction must be brought from memory before anything can be done with it, so fetch always comes first.

questions.text: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be executed?
questions.solution: The program counter tracks where execution has reached. The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded, not its address.

questions.text: During the fetch phase, the contents of the program counter are first transferred to
questions.solution: Memory is addressed through the MAR, so the PC value goes there first. The word that comes back arrives in the MBR and is then moved into the instruction register.

questions.text: In the ideal case, what speedup does a k-stage instruction pipeline offer over a non-pipelined implementation?
questions.solution: With k stages full and no stalls, k instructions are in flight at once and one completes per cycle, so throughput improves k-fold. Stage imbalance, latch overhead and hazards keep real speedup below k.

questions.text: A 5-stage pipeline with one cycle per stage executes 100 instructions with no stalls. How many clock cycles does it take in total?
questions.solution: The first instruction takes k = 5 cycles to fill the pipeline and each of the remaining 99 completes one cycle later: 5 + 99 = 104.

questions.text: The clock period of a pipelined processor is determined by

options.text: the slowest stage plus the latch delay
the average of the stage delays
the sum of all stage delays

questions.solution: Every stage advances on the same edge, so the clock must be slow enough for the worst one, plus the time to latch results between stages. This is why balancing stages matters more than making one of them fast.

questions.text: A non-pipelined processor takes 100 ns per instruction. It is redesigned as a 5-stage pipeline with equal stage delays plus a 2 ns latch delay per stage. What is the maximum speedup for a large number of instructions? Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution: Each stage takes 100/5 = 20 ns, and with the latch the clock period is 22 ns. For many instructions the pipeline retires one per cycle, so the speedup is 100/22 = 4.55, short of the ideal 5 because of the latch overhead.

questions.text: A branch instruction whose outcome is not yet known causes which kind of pipeline hazard?
questions.solution: The pipeline does not know which instruction to fetch next until the branch resolves. Branch prediction and delayed branches exist to limit the cost.

questions.text: A read-after-write (RAW) hazard is also known as
questions.solution: The second instruction genuinely needs the value the first produces, so the dependency is real and cannot be removed by renaming registers, unlike WAR and WAW.

questions.text: Operand forwarding (bypassing) in a pipeline is used to

options.text: pass a result to a later stage before it is written to the register file

questions.solution: The value already exists in a pipeline latch, so routing it straight to the stage that needs it avoids waiting for the write-back. It removes most RAW stalls, though a load-use hazard can still cost a cycle.

questions.text: A WAR (write-after-read) hazard arises when

options.text: an instruction writes a location that an earlier instruction has not yet read
two instructions write the same location
an instruction reads a location an earlier instruction has not yet written
two instructions need the same functional unit

questions.solution: It is an anti-dependency: the later write would destroy a value the earlier instruction still needs. It only appears when instructions can complete out of order, and register renaming removes it.

questions.text: Cache memory works because programs exhibit
questions.solution: Programs reuse recently used addresses (temporal locality) and use addresses near them (spatial locality), so a small fast memory can capture most accesses.

questions.text: A cache has an access time of 10 ns and main memory 100 ns. On a miss the word is supplied from main memory. With a hit ratio of 0.9, what is the average access time in nanoseconds, taking it as h x 10 + (1 - h) x 100?
questions.solution: 0.9 x 10 + 0.1 x 100 = 9 + 10 = 19 ns. Even a 10% miss rate contributes more than the hits do, which is why miss rate dominates cache design.

questions.text: In a direct-mapped cache, a given block of main memory

options.text: can be placed in exactly one cache line
can be placed in any cache line
can be placed in any line within one set

questions.solution: The index bits of the address fix the line, so placement needs no search and no replacement policy. The cost is conflict misses when two hot blocks share an index.

questions.text: A byte-addressable machine has 32-bit addresses. A direct-mapped cache has 512 lines with a block size of 32 bytes. How many tag bits does each line need?
questions.solution: A 32-byte block needs 5 offset bits, and 512 lines need 9 index bits. The tag takes the rest: 32 - 9 - 5 = 18 bits.

questions.text: Which write policy updates main memory only when a modified block is evicted?
questions.solution: Write back marks the line dirty and defers the memory write, saving bandwidth when a line is written repeatedly. Write through updates memory on every write, keeping the two always consistent.

questions.text: In a fully associative cache, an incoming block

options.text: may be placed in any line
may be placed in only one line
may be placed only in line 0
is placed by hashing the tag

questions.solution: Any line will do, which eliminates conflict misses but requires every tag to be compared in parallel. That comparison cost is why fully associative caches stay small.

questions.text: A cache organised as 8 sets with 4 lines in each set is described as
questions.solution: The associativity is the number of lines per set, so four lines per set makes it 4-way. The set is chosen by index bits, and the tag is then compared against the four lines in it.

questions.text: A 2-way set associative cache has 128 lines in total. How many sets does it have?
questions.solution: Sets = lines / associativity = 128 / 2 = 64.

questions.text: Which of the following has the shortest access time?
questions.solution: Registers sit inside the datapath and are reachable within a single cycle. The hierarchy trades speed against capacity and cost at every level below them.

questions.text: How many bytes are there in 1 KiB (kibibyte)?
questions.solution: Memory sizes are powers of two because addresses are binary: 1 KiB = 2^10 = 1024 bytes.

questions.text: DRAM must be refreshed periodically because

options.text: each bit is stored on a capacitor whose charge leaks away
it has no power supply of its own

questions.solution: A DRAM cell is one transistor and one capacitor, and the charge decays within milliseconds, so each row must be read and rewritten. SRAM uses cross-coupled transistors that hold their state as long as power is applied.

questions.text: Direct memory access (DMA) allows

options.text: an I/O device to transfer data to or from memory without the CPU handling each word
the CPU to access memory faster
two processors to share a cache
programs to address more memory than is installed

questions.solution: The DMA controller drives the bus itself, so the CPU is involved only in setting up the transfer and handling its completion.

questions.text: In cycle stealing mode, a DMA controller

options.text: takes the bus for one word at a time, between CPU accesses
holds the bus until the entire block is transferred
transfers data only when the CPU is halted

questions.solution: One word is moved per stolen cycle, so the CPU is slowed but never stopped for long. Burst mode, by contrast, holds the bus for the whole block and gives the fastest transfer.

questions.text: How does the CPU learn that a DMA transfer has finished?

options.text: The DMA controller raises an interrupt
The CPU polls the memory contents
The transfer count register is copied into the accumulator
It does not need to know

questions.solution: When the word count reaches zero the controller interrupts the CPU, which is the whole point: the processor does useful work during the transfer instead of waiting.

questions.text: Which is a characteristic of RISC architectures?

options.text: Instructions that operate directly on memory operands

questions.solution: Fixed-length instructions make fetching and decoding regular, which is what allows straightforward pipelining. The other three options describe CISC.

questions.text: In a load-store architecture, memory is accessed

options.text: only by load and store instructions

questions.solution: Arithmetic works register to register, so only loads and stores touch memory. That keeps every arithmetic instruction the same length in cycles, which suits a pipeline.

questions.text: Compared with RISC, a CISC processor typically has

options.text: more instructions and more addressing modes, often with micro-programmed control
a larger register file and fixed instruction length

questions.solution: CISC puts complexity in the hardware, using micro-programmed control to implement a rich instruction set. RISC pushes that complexity to the compiler and keeps control hardwired.

questions.text: Compared with micro-programmed control, hardwired control is
questions.solution: Control signals come straight from combinational logic, so there is no control-memory lookup. Changing the instruction set means redesigning that logic.

questions.text: In a micro-programmed control unit, the control signals for each step are held in
questions.solution: Each micro-instruction in control memory names the signals to assert for one step, and a micro-program counter walks through them. Altering behaviour becomes a matter of rewriting the micro-program.

questions.text: Which control unit design is normally preferred for a RISC processor?
questions.solution: A small, regular instruction set is simple enough to decode in combinational logic, and the speed matters more than the flexibility a micro-program would buy.

questions.text: In memory-mapped I/O,

options.text: device registers occupy addresses in the ordinary memory address space
special IN and OUT instructions are required
devices are accessed only through DMA
the operating system copies data through the accumulator

questions.solution: Device registers look like memory, so ordinary load and store instructions reach them and no separate I/O instructions are needed. The cost is that those addresses are no longer available for memory.

questions.text: The main drawback of programmed I/O (polling) is that

options.text: the CPU wastes time repeatedly testing the device status
it cannot transfer more than one byte

questions.solution: The processor sits in a loop reading a status register while the device works, so its time is spent waiting rather than computing.

questions.text: An I/O processor (channel) differs from a DMA controller in that it

options.text: executes its own sequence of I/O instructions from memory
interrupts the CPU for every word

questions.solution: A channel runs an I/O program, so it can carry out a whole sequence of transfers and conditional steps on its own. A DMA controller only performs the single transfer it was configured for.

questions.text: Interrupt-driven I/O improves on polling because

options.text: the device signals the CPU when it is ready, so the CPU can do other work meanwhile
it transfers data faster per byte
it avoids the use of buses

questions.solution: The initiative moves to the device, so the processor is interrupted only when there is something to do rather than checking continually.
